title: Smoke in the Skins
passage:
The fires came down the range in the third week of January, and by Saturday half the growers in the district had sprinklers running along the rows. Ash lay on the leaves in grey drifts, the fruit was a fortnight from picking, and hosing a dirty thing clean is what anybody would try. Corin Pemberdine, who runs the laboratory most of them use, made a trial of it: two blocks washed down, two left alone, all four picked and fermented in the same shed that afternoon. It made no difference. One washed lot even read a little higher than the block beside it, though Pemberdine will not build on a single pair. By then there was nothing on the outside of a berry left to wash off.

Wood smoke carries a family of small molecules called volatile phenols – guaiacol and the cresols among them – set free when the lignin in the wood comes apart in the heat. They cross the waxy skin of a grape within hours. Once they are inside, the berry joins a sugar to each one, as it does with other foreign compounds, and the result is a glycoside: odourless, and unable to evaporate. Most of it stays in the skin. Pemberdine puts the window at a day or two. After that the fruit carries its smoke in a locked form, and what a nose can find in the juice is a small remainder. Four weeks after the fires his laboratory was finding nine parts bound for every part free. Leaves take the phenols up too, but what a leaf takes up stays in the leaf. They matter only when they reach the fermenter with the grapes, which is why the district picks by hand after a fire.

That is the awkward part for anyone judging affected fruit by nose. Tamsin Quennerly, who runs a tasting panel of twenty-four, describes January wines that gave the nose very little and then turned dry and ashy half a minute after they were swallowed. The sugar comes off in the mouth. Enzymes in saliva, and the bacteria alongside them, cut the phenol loose, and it reaches the nose from behind, after the glass has been put down. Her panel does not agree with itself about how much of it there is. Six of the twenty-four mark the ashy finish harder than the rest, year after year; one tasted the worst lot of the vintage and called it clean. Quennerly is untroubled by the spread. “The median is the only figure that has ever predicted what a drinker will say,” she says, “and a reading that contradicts it should give way.” She is right about that. The January readings were unremarkable and the January wines were not.

Two other rules of thumb have not survived either. Growers were told for years that smoke before véraison did not count, until a season in which fruit smoked a fortnight before the colour turned produced wine that the panel marked down. The advice has been withdrawn, though the weeks after véraison are still the worst time to be downwind. Thickness of smoke is no guide either. Pemberdine’s instruments logged the particulate load hour by hour, and that record does not follow what turned up in the fruit. “A number tells you the fruit met smoke,” he says. “It does not tell you what the wine will be.” There is also a delay nobody has an answer for. Acid works slowly on a glycoside, so a wine can pass at bottling and be ashy at eighteen months. Two of the January reds have done exactly that.

What the district does now is small and unglamorous. Growers ferment five kilograms from each block in a shed the week before picking, and taste it warm out of a jar, because ten days of that is the shortest honest test anybody has. It is the sensible answer, and it is still too slow for a fire that comes in the last fortnight. Pemberdine wants a threshold a grower could act on sooner. Quennerly thinks any threshold will be wrong in both directions, and would spend the money on more tasters. Forty tonnes went on the ground in March, on a reading and a nervous buyer. Nobody will now find out what that fruit would have made.
– Rhodri Kettlestrand, staff writer

véraison = the point in the season when grapes change colour and begin to ripen in earnest
glycoside = a compound formed when a sugar is joined chemically to another molecule

questions.prompt: What are we told about the blocks that were hosed down?

options.text: Hosing removes some of the smoke if it is done within a day of a fire.
Their wine was no different, and one of them measured slightly higher than its neighbour.
Their fruit held less of the smoke compounds, though the wine tasted much the same.
Pemberdine put the higher of the two washed readings down to ash blown back onto the bunches.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 1. WHY-KEY (B): the passage reports that the four lots were picked and fermented together and that the washing "made no difference", and then adds the awkward particular that "One washed lot even read a little higher than the block beside it". B carries both halves in different words and claims nothing further. The second half is the part a reader must actually have read: it is an invented detail of this trial, not something a solver could supply from general knowledge about washing fruit. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier/condition graft with a hedge that makes it sound careful – it borrows the real "day or two" window from paragraph 2, which is the time the berry takes to bolt a sugar onto the phenols, and misapplies it to washing; the passage defeats it twice over, since the phenols "cross the waxy skin of a grape within hours" and by then "there was nothing on the outside of a berry left to wash off". Tempting because it is the only option that sounds appropriately qualified. C = half-right conjunction – the second clause is true (the wine tasted the same) while the first is contradicted by the one washed lot that read higher; nothing in the passage says washed fruit held less. It is also the trap that punishes outside knowledge, since a reader who has met the misting literature will recognise the shape "less compound, same taste" and import it. D = invented attribution – the passage says the opposite, that Pemberdine "will not build on a single pair"; tempting because the reading is real and a cause for it is the natural thing to want.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the leaves of the vines?

options.text: They carry the phenols through to the bunches.
They release the phenols again as they dry.
They are stripped off before a smoke-affected harvest.
They take up the phenols and keep them there.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 2; this is the unit's short-breath item (short stem, options of eight or nine words). WHY-KEY (D): "Leaves take the phenols up too, but what a leaf takes up stays in the leaf." D paraphrases exactly that and stops there. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = reversed direction of transfer, the single most tempting error in the paragraph, because the sentence does say leaves take phenols up and a reader who stops at the comma will complete it the intuitive way; the clause after the comma is the whole point. B = plausible outside knowledge the passage never states – nothing is said about leaves giving anything back to the air as they dry, and the passage's only reason for caring about leaves is the fermenter. C = outside knowledge in the form of a real viticultural practice: leaf plucking is a familiar vineyard operation, but this passage prescribes hand-picking, and it does so to keep leaves out of the fermenter, not to strip them off the vine before harvest.

questions.prompt: What is implied by the disagreement inside Quennerly’s panel?

options.text: The six who mark hardest are more sensitive to smoke in the air than the rest.
An ashy finish belongs to the wine alone, and a trained taster will always find it.
Some of the ashy finish is made in the taster’s own mouth, not the glass.
Panels of this kind cannot be trusted, and the laboratory should decide instead.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (C): the passage gives the mechanism – enzymes in saliva and the bacteria alongside them cut the phenol loose, so the smell arrives "from behind, after the glass has been put down" – and then reports that six of twenty-four mark the finish harder year after year while one called the worst lot of the vintage clean. Put together, the release happens in the mouth, and mouths differ; so part of what is scored is contributed by the taster. That is one step from the text and no further. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = locus shift, the same six tasters transferred from the palate to the nose; the passage is explicit that these wines "gave the nose very little", so a difference in what the six smell in the air is precisely what the paragraph rules out. B = reversal plus absolute, the position the paragraph is written against; the spread and the taster who called the worst lot clean both contradict it. It is the key’s chief rival for a careless reader. D = two-step leap – a real conclusion someone might draw from a split panel, but the passage puts the median above the reading ("the only figure that has ever predicted what a drinker will say") and reports that the January readings were unremarkable while the wines were not.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude towards the laboratory readings?

options.text: He backs the panel outright where its verdict and a reading disagree.
He shares the chemist’s hope that a workable threshold will soon be found.
He sets the two positions side by side and leaves the choice to the reader.
He treats the testing as an expense the growers would be better off without.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude), whole-text item, signature trap role_or_attribution_swap. WHY-KEY (A): the writer's own voice enters three times and each time it takes a side. After Quennerly's claim that a contradicting reading "should give way" he writes "She is right about that", and supplies the evidence himself in the next sentence ("The January readings were unremarkable and the January wines were not"). He then calls the shed ferments – a tasting test – "the sensible answer". Nothing hedges the endorsement; A states it as flatly as he does. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = role_or_attribution_swap – the wish for an earlier threshold is Pemberdine's, given in the closing paragraph in his own name and immediately met by Quennerly's objection that any threshold will be wrong in both directions; the writer never adopts it. It is the trap for a reader who takes the last technical voice in a passage for the writer's. C = tone_misread, and the option a form-only reader picks because it sounds like the judicious answer a reporter ought to give; the sentence "She is right about that" is exactly what a writer leaving the choice to the reader would not write. D = polarity overshoot – he credits the laboratory with settling the hosing question, quotes its bound-to-free measurement without demur, and lets Pemberdine state his own limits; contempt for the testing is nowhere in the passage.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The trial in which some blocks were hosed down after the fires and others left alone.
How grapes store smoke in a form the nose cannot find, and what that costs growers.
How the phenols in wood smoke are formed when the lignin in a log breaks down.
The losses that fire seasons impose on growers and the arguments with buyers that follow.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (B): every paragraph turns on the same fact and its consequences – the sugar the berry bolts onto the phenol, which makes the compound odourless and unable to evaporate. That is why hosing is futile, why a nose finds only a small remainder in the juice, why the panel meets the wines on the palate and not on the nose, why a wine can pass at bottling and turn at eighteen months, and why the district now hand-picks and ferments five kilograms in a shed before it will commit to picking. B names the hidden form and the practical cost together, which is the shape of the whole piece. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error – the hosing trial is the opening paragraph only, and it functions as the way into the mechanism rather than as the subject; a reader who weights the first vivid scene picks it. C = surface_word_match – it recycles the passage's most distinctive vocabulary (phenols, lignin) into a topic the text disposes of in a single subordinate clause; the chemistry of combustion is not what any of the five paragraphs is about. D = outside_knowledge – true-sounding, and the closing sentence does mention a nervous buyer and forty tonnes on the ground, but the passage never argues about losses or describes any dispute with a buyer; it is the article a reader might expect from the topic rather than the one in front of them.

generator_meta.science_verification: The mechanism was checked against the literature before the passage was written, because batch15's ELF short was refuted at V-FINAL for stating a physical mechanism backwards. Verified 2026-08-26 via Exa web search (WebSearch budget was exhausted at 200/200 before any query, so Exa was used throughout; every claim below is re-runnable): (1) smoke's volatile phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, o-/m-/p-cresol, syringol) come from pyrolysis of lignin/lignocellulose - Molecules 26(15):4519; (2) primary entry is directly through the waxy cuticle of the berry, phenols also enter leaves, but no significant translocation from leaf to berry is observed - AWRI fact sheet 'Smoke taint - entry into grapes and vineyard risk factors' (updated Oct 2025); leaf material matters because it carries phenols into the fermenter as MOG - OSU Extension EM 9253, Washington State Wine Commission smoke FAQ; (3) the berry rapidly glycosylates the phenols via glycosyltransferases into non-volatile, odourless glycosides held mainly in the skins - Molecules 26(15):4519, J Nat Prod 2022 (PMC8961875); Wine Australia puts the practical window at roughly 48 hours; (4) washing/hosing does not remove the taint because the compounds are already inside the skin cells, and high-pressure washing 'may even make it worse' - Wine Australia 'Smoke damage'; a controlled in-canopy misting trial lowered some grape phenol concentrations yet did not change the sensory outcome - Molecules/PMC7464031; (5) release in the mouth by salivary enzymes and oral bacteria gives the delayed ashy retronasal aftertaste, with strong dependence on the individual taster - Mayr et al. via Krstic et al. 2015 review (Aust J Grape Wine Res 21:537-553), Parker et al. 2012, PMC8961875; (6) the week after veraison to harvest is the highest-risk window, but the older rule that pre-veraison smoke is harmless was withdrawn after the 2019/20 Australian events - AWRI fact sheet, Beverages 2021 7(1):7 review; (7) particulate-matter density does not track what gets into the fruit - PMC7464031, AWRI; (8) glycosides hydrolyse slowly under wine's acidity, so guaiacol rises over years in bottle - Singh et al. 2011 via Krstic et al. 2015. The passage asserts nothing beyond this set; all figures, dates, people and events built on top of it are invented.
